market_context: United States/Canada; identifying and preventing drain flies by removing organic film, correcting leaks and avoiding extermination-focused treatment.
title: What to Do About Drain Flies and How to Keep Them From Coming Back

seo.title: Drain Flies: Where They Come From and How to Keep Them From Returning
seo.meta_description: Drain flies often develop in wet organic film inside plumbing or around leaks. Learn how to locate the source, clean it out and prevent recurrence.
seo.search_intent: Resolve recurring drain flies by identifying and removing the damp organic breeding source.

excerpt: If tiny fuzzy flies gather around a sink, shower or tub, the source is often moist organic film inside the drain. The durable fix is to physically scrub away that film, keep the plumbing clean and correct leaks or hidden moisture. Bleach or boiling water may change activity briefly but usually does not remove the material where the flies develop.
content_html:
Drain flies can seem to appear from nowhere because you usually notice them on a wall or mirror rather than inside the pipe supporting them. They are tiny, somewhat fuzzy and often look like miniature moths. They tend to collect near sinks, tubs, showers, floor drains and other damp areas.

The lasting solution is not targeting the adults you can see. It is finding and removing the wet organic film where the immature stages are developing.

First confirm that a drain is really the source

Watch where activity is strongest, especially after the room has been quiet for several hours. If the flies consistently gather around one drain, start there.

You can place a clear container loosely over the opening during a period when the drain will not be used, while leaving the plumbing system safe and unobstructed. If activity repeatedly points to that opening, you have a strong clue. The goal is observation, not trapping.

Drain flies do not live on “water” alone

University of Minnesota Extension explains that drain flies lay eggs in moist organic material and that larvae commonly live in the gelatinous film inside sink, shower and tub drains.

That explains why simply pouring liquid down the pipe may do little. Water passes through the center while the film remains attached to the pipe wall.

Physically remove the film

Remove the strainer or stopper if the design allows and use a long, narrow brush suitable for plumbing to scrub reachable interior surfaces. Clean the overflow channel on a sink too if it has visible buildup.

The goal is to dislodge slime, hair, soap and organic residue rather than merely deodorize the pipe. Rinse afterward using a method appropriate for the fixture.

The trap may hold residue too

If activity continues and the P-trap is accessible, it may need cleaning. Put a bucket underneath, open only serviceable connections and check carefully for leaks after reassembly.

Do not open a trap after recently using a corrosive drain cleaner. Chemical can remain pooled in the bend and splash when the connection is loosened.

Why boiling water usually does not solve the problem

Colorado State University Extension notes that hot or boiling water does not do a good job of removing the bacterial and organic film where these flies develop.

It may rinse loose material, but it does not replace scrubbing. Very hot water can also be unsuitable for some piping, seals or fixtures, so it should not be treated as a universal drain treatment.

Bleach is not a substitute for cleaning either

University of Minnesota notes that bleach and standard chemical drain cleaners are not effective by themselves when the organic layer remains attached to the drain walls.

If you use any cleaning product, follow its label and never mix chemicals. The main job is still to remove the source material physically.

Do not forget rarely used drains

Floor drains, utility sinks and guest bathrooms can hold moisture and residue for long periods. Check them if you clean the main bathroom or kitchen drain but still see flies.

Also make sure traps that are supposed to contain water have not dried out. A dry trap can allow sewer odors and gases into the room and deserves separate plumbing attention.

If they are not coming from the drain, look for a leak

Drain flies can also develop where contaminated water or wet organic material exists outside an open fixture. A leak under a cabinet, behind a wall or around damaged plumbing can create a hidden source.

If flies seem to emerge from floor joints or wall gaps, there is a persistent sewer odor or activity continues after all accessible drains are cleaned, investigate a plumbing or sanitation problem.

A visibly clean bathroom can still have drain flies

Clean tile, fixtures and floors tell you nothing about the inside wall of a drain. A thin layer of organic film can remain completely out of sight.

That does not mean the home is generally dirty. It means the cleaning needs to reach the specific damp location supporting the flies.

How to keep them from returning

Remove hair and residue before it moves deeper into the drain, clean strainers and stoppers, fix drips and do not let organic material build for months in rarely used fixtures.

If a drain begins to smell or slow down, address the buildup early rather than waiting for a thick layer to form.

When to call a professional

Get help if activity continues after thorough cleaning, seems to come from under a slab or behind a wall, accompanies a sewage odor, affects several drains or suggests a broken sewer or drain line.

In those cases, the flies are a secondary clue to a moisture or sanitation problem that matters on its own.

The idea that stops the cycle

You do not need to treat the entire room. Identify the drain or damp source, scrub away the organic film, check the trap and overflow, and correct any leak.

Once the wet place where the flies can develop is gone, there is no new generation to keep appearing on the wall a few days later.

faq.question: Where do drain flies come from?
faq.answer: They usually develop in moist organic film inside drains, traps or other areas where leaking water and decaying material remain wet.

faq.question: Does boiling water get rid of drain flies?
faq.answer: It usually does not remove the attached organic film and may not be suitable for all plumbing materials. Mechanical cleaning matters more.

faq.question: Will bleach solve drain flies?
faq.answer: Not by itself if the organic layer remains inside the pipe. Never mix bleach with other drain products.

faq.question: Why do they keep coming back after I clean the sink?
faq.answer: The source may be deeper in the drain, in the overflow, another rarely used drain or a hidden leak.
